messages.content: You are an autonomous Formula 1 forecaster. Use your judgment and tools to produce the most accurate, well-calibrated full-field race probabilities possible. Follow the output contract exactly.

Make the single pre-race forecast for 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix — Baku.

Use all public information available at the time of this run. Decide for yourself how to research, reason, write code, build models, or simulate. `web-search` finds sources and `web-extract` reads pages; both have `--help`.

/history is read-only and contains your earlier race predictions, research reports, official results, scores, and post-race reviews when available. Read your notes first, then examine relevant past races to understand recent form and whether earlier lessons still hold. /memory/notes.md is your only persistent writable memory; review or update it if useful. /workspace is disposable scratch space.

Drivers:
- NOR: Lando Norris (McLaren)
- PIA: Oscar Piastri (McLaren)
- RUS: George Russell (Mercedes)
- ANT: Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)
- VER: Max Verstappen (Red Bull Racing)
- HAD: Isack Hadjar (Red Bull Racing)
- LEC: Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)
- HAM: Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)
- ALB: Alexander Albon (Williams)
- SAI: Carlos Sainz (Williams)
- LIN: Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)
- LAW: Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)
- STR: Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)
- ALO: Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)
- OCO: Esteban Ocon (Haas)
- BEA: Oliver Bearman (Haas)
- HUL: Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)
- BOR: Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi)
- GAS: Pierre Gasly (Alpine)
- COL: Franco Colapinto (Alpine)
- PER: Sergio Perez (Cadillac)
- BOT: Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)

/output/prediction.json is already filled with the exact schema. Replace every null with a probability. Do not add fields. The positions array is P1 through P22. For each driver, positions + nc + dns + dsq must sum to 1; retirement is a separate probability. Every value must be finite and within [0, 1]. Across drivers, each position's total cannot exceed 1, and later-position occupancy cannot exceed earlier-position occupancy.

Your job is to predict where every driver lands, with defensible reasoning. Research the current grid and penalties, weekend pace, circuit, strategy, weather and reliability. Prefer primary sources; distinguish facts, inference and missing evidence. Check publication times and verify consequential claims. Do not invent sources or assume research snippets are reliable. Betting markets may be a cross-check, but disclose their influence and make your own case.

Use modeling only when it improves the call. Challenge your strongest assumption with a plausible alternative scenario and explain which drivers move. Compare your order with the starting grid: justify material departures and explain why track position holds elsewhere. A similar order is acceptable. Do not manufacture surprises, causal certainty, or complexity to look sophisticated. Spend effort resolving consequential uncertainty, not filling the time budget.

Also write /output/report.json with this exact readable structure:
{"event_id": "2026-15-azerbaijan", "summary": "Your central race call", "order": ["driver IDs, each exactly once, best to worst"], "reasons": {"driver ID": "Brief reason for this driver's place, including material risks"}, "method": "What research/calculations you used, what they changed, and any market influence", "uncertainty": "Strongest assumption, alternative scenario and drivers affected", "insights": [{"claim": "A specific evidence-based judgment; no clear edge is acceptable", "impact": "How it changes your forecast", "check": "What observable race evidence would support or weaken this explanation", "sources": ["s1"]}], "sources": [{"id": "s1", "title": "Source title", "url": "https://..."}]}

The order is your single full-field call, including drivers exposed to retirement; probabilities still represent all possible outcomes and are what get scored. Keep the order and reasons consistent with them. Provide a few useful insights, not a generic weekend recap. Source references are required; they do not substitute for reasoning. The report must be valid JSON. You may additionally write /output/explanation.md for longer calculations. Create no other files under /output. Validate your work carefully. When finished, run `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT` alone.

--- /memory/notes.md
# Forecast notes

## 2026-14 Madrid pre-race (forecast made 2026-09-13 07:30 UTC)
- FIA grid: NOR ANT VER HAM LEC RUS PIA LAW COL LIN HUL BOR OCO GAS TSU ALB ALO PER BOT SAI BEA STR. SAI 3-place penalty; STR 40-place PU penalty; BEA/STR permitted to start.
- Weekend: Mercedes strongest high-fuel evidence (RUS benchmark, VER +0.13s adjusted); NOR pole by 0.011 but no useful FP2 long run after gearbox issue. Hot/dry. Severe graining and 0.2-0.3s/lap Friday degradation versus ~24s pit loss; overtaking very difficult.
- Market calibration at cutoff: Polymarket raw mids ANT .40, NOR .35, VER .12, HAM .065, RUS .0445, LEC .029, PIA .017. Final model P1 approximately .379/.345/.114/.063/.043/.030/.015.
- Used mixture of processional, high-degradation, and chaotic regimes; expected 4.82 retirements. Elevated STR failure risk (.47 retirement, .04 DNS), BEA .31/.015 after rebuild. Late retirements can retain numbered classifications.
- Check official result later for calibration, especially whether 25% chaos weighting and midfield top-10 spread were too broad.

## 2026-14 Madrid post-race (official result)
- Result: ANT-VER-NOR-LEC-RUS-LAW-COL-PIA-LIN-HUL; NC SAI/PER/STR/HAM. ANT was the 37.9% P1 favourite, the three highest podium probabilities made the exact podium, and 9/10 drivers with the highest points probabilities scored (HUL, ranked 12th at 45.6%, replaced HAM). The central pace/order model was strong; do not materially retune it from this race.
- Separate outcome from pace: NOR led by about 4.5s and had the best managed race pace. A Lap-13 VSC began just after he passed pit entry, gave ANT/VER cheap stops, and ended before NOR returned; his subsequent 7s stop compounded the loss. ANT winning is neutralisation/pit-stop variance, not proof that the sparse Friday long-run signal correctly put Mercedes ahead. Keep adjusted short practice runs heavily shrunk and treat a missing run as uncertainty, not negative evidence.
- Friday graining/degradation did not translate directly: difficult passing, a ~24s stop loss, track evolution and managed pace made one stop dominant, while the little-used Hard stayed consistent for 45+ laps. At new tracks, condition multi-stop/high-degradation weight on passing incentives and likely management, and retain wider priors for untested compounds.
- Model VSC/SC timing jointly with track location, starting compound and pit windows rather than only adding generic “chaos” dispersion; even a very short VSC produced large, correlated strategy gains/losses in an otherwise processional race.
- Tail check, not a pace update: PIA's P8 had only 2.97% exact probability (largest log-loss miss) after Lap-1 front-wing damage, traffic and an adverse VSC. On low-overtaking tracks, ensure repairable contact carries enough classified multi-place downside mass rather than routing most adverse mass to retirement. HAM's brake DNF was a plausible 10.8% NC tail, not evidence to demote his pace.
- Reliability level was sound: 4 retirements versus 4.82 expected (4.34 expected NC), retirement Brier 0.1410. Elevated STR/PER risks helped, but their realised causes do not cleanly validate every causal prior; do not retune individuals from one draw. Audit all post-crash rebuilds consistently by repair scope and successful subsequent mileage; Hamilton's brake root cause was unconfirmed.
- Longitudinal score baseline: mean RPS 0.09592, log loss 2.03034, win/podium/points Brier 0.02385/0.02940/0.10344, expected-rank MAE 3.268.

# 2026 Spanish Grand Prix (MADRING) pre-race forecast

**Forecast cut-off:** 13 September 2026, approximately 07:30 UTC (race start 13:00 UTC).

## Evidence used

- The FIA provisional grid puts Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen, Hamilton, Leclerc, Russell, Piastri and Lawson in the first eight places. Sainz drops to P20 for impeding Bottas; Bearman and Stroll are permitted to start P21/P22; Stroll has a 40-place power-unit penalty. [FIA Document 57](https://www.fia.com/system/files/decision-document/2026_spanish_grand_prix_-_provisional_starting_grid.pdf) and [permission-to-start decision](https://www.fia.com/system/files/decision-document/2026_spanish_grand_prix_-_decision_-_permission_to_start.pdf).
- Norris beat Antonelli by only 0.011 seconds in Q3, with Verstappen 0.140s from pole and the first seven covered by 0.470s. Earlier phases and all three practices pointed more strongly toward Mercedes than Norris's exceptional final lap alone. [Official qualifying report](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/norris-denies-antonelli-pole-position-for-spanish-gp-in-closely-fought-qualifying-in-madrid.5AqJXaE8s1sLfv8dJVLqty).
- Friday's short, traffic-affected long runs made Russell the benchmark. Motorsport's compound/stint-adjusted analysis had Verstappen about 0.13s per lap behind, Antonelli 0.55s behind, the Ferraris around 0.9s behind and Piastri 1.51s behind. Norris had no representative high-fuel run after a gearbox problem. [Motorsport.com long-run analysis](https://www.motorsport.com/f1/news/mercedes-clearly-ahead-how-long-run-pace-compared-in-f1-spanish-gp-practice-/10854723/).
- The strategic evidence is unusually uncertain. Pirelli measured roughly 0.2–0.3s/lap degradation and front-left graining, but the green-flag pit loss is about 24 seconds and overtaking was extremely difficult in the support races. Medium-Hard is the natural one-stop; Medium-Hard-Hard remains competitive if Friday's degradation persists. [F1 team/Pirelli Saturday comments](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/what-the-teams-said-qualifying-in-spain-2026.014qyfNipmqu7dP0ZuCvfc) and [strategy analysis](https://www.the-race.com/formula-1/f1-teams-face-big-madring-strategy-dilemma/).
- The race is forecast to be hot, clear and dry, around 32°C ambient with a possible 53°C track temperature. [Motorsport.com weather preview](https://www.motorsport.com/f1/news/f1-spanish-gp-at-madring-sunday-schedule-weather-forecast-and-how-to-watch/10855127/).
- Post-qualifying market prices were used as an external calibration rather than as the model itself. At the cut-off, the liquid Polymarket mid-prices were approximately Antonelli 40%, Norris 35%, Verstappen 12%, Hamilton 6.5%, Russell 4.45%, Leclerc 2.9% and Piastri 1.7% before normalization; sportsbook prices showed a similar front-row concentration. [Polymarket event](https://polymarket.com/event/f1-spanish-grand-prix-winner-2026-09-13) and [post-qualifying odds snapshot](https://www.thespread.com/auto-racing/2026-f1-spanish-grand-prix-predictions-and-picks-our-best-bets-for-madring/).

## Method and interpretation

I combined the 13 completed 2026 Grands Prix, recent form, grid position, weekend pace and driver/team reliability in a Monte Carlo rank model. Because this is MADRING's first Grand Prix, outcomes were mixed across three latent race shapes: a track-position-led one-stop race, a high-degradation strategic race, and a Safety Car/red-flag-heavy race. Team-level pace uncertainty, starts, strategy errors, non-terminal incidents and correlated race conditions broaden the positional tails.

The resulting win probabilities are led by **Antonelli (37.89%)**, **Norris (34.51%)**, **Verstappen (11.38%)**, **Hamilton (6.27%)**, **Russell (4.34%)**, **Leclerc (3.03%)** and **Piastri (1.47%)**. Norris has the track-position advantage; Antonelli gets a narrow overall edge from Mercedes' high-fuel evidence and season-long strength.

Retirement risk is above a normal dry-race baseline because the circuit is wall-lined and unfamiliar, practice produced several heavy crashes, support racing produced a first-lap pile-up, and 2026 reliability has been poor. Stroll is the largest individual risk after repeated Honda failures and this weekend's fresh-PU water-pressure problem; Bearman also carries extra DNS/retirement risk while Haas rebuilds the car after his FP3 impact. The model averages about **4.82 race retirements**.

`retirement` is modeled separately from classification. A driver retiring late can still receive a numbered FIA classification; earlier retirements go to `nc`. `dns` includes failure to take the start, while `dsq` is a small separate post-event risk.

# Forecast notes

## 2026-14 Madrid pre-race (forecast made 2026-09-13 07:30 UTC)
- FIA grid: NOR ANT VER HAM LEC RUS PIA LAW COL LIN HUL BOR OCO GAS TSU ALB ALO PER BOT SAI BEA STR. SAI 3-place penalty; STR 40-place PU penalty; BEA/STR permitted to start.
- Weekend: Mercedes strongest high-fuel evidence (RUS benchmark, VER +0.13s adjusted); NOR pole by 0.011 but no useful FP2 long run after gearbox issue. Hot/dry. Severe graining and 0.2-0.3s/lap Friday degradation versus ~24s pit loss; overtaking very difficult.
- Market calibration at cutoff: Polymarket raw mids ANT .40, NOR .35, VER .12, HAM .065, RUS .0445, LEC .029, PIA .017. Final model P1 approximately .379/.345/.114/.063/.043/.030/.015.
- Used mixture of processional, high-degradation, and chaotic regimes; expected 4.82 retirements. Elevated STR failure risk (.47 retirement, .04 DNS), BEA .31/.015 after rebuild. Late retirements can retain numbered classifications.
- Check official result later for calibration, especially whether 25% chaos weighting and midfield top-10 spread were too broad.

## 2026-14 Madrid post-race (official result)
- Result: ANT-VER-NOR-LEC-RUS-LAW-COL-PIA-LIN-HUL; NC SAI/PER/STR/HAM. ANT was the 37.9% P1 favourite, the three highest podium probabilities made the exact podium, and 9/10 drivers with the highest points probabilities scored (HUL, ranked 12th at 45.6%, replaced HAM). The central pace/order model was strong; do not materially retune it from this race.
- Separate outcome from pace: NOR led by about 4.5s and had the best managed race pace. A Lap-13 VSC began just after he passed pit entry, gave ANT/VER cheap stops, and ended before NOR returned; his subsequent 7s stop compounded the loss. ANT winning is neutralisation/pit-stop variance, not proof that the sparse Friday long-run signal correctly put Mercedes ahead. Keep adjusted short practice runs heavily shrunk and treat a missing run as uncertainty, not negative evidence.
- Friday graining/degradation did not translate directly: difficult passing, a ~24s stop loss, track evolution and managed pace made one stop dominant, while the little-used Hard stayed consistent for 45+ laps. At new tracks, condition multi-stop/high-degradation weight on passing incentives and likely management, and retain wider priors for untested compounds.
- Model VSC/SC timing jointly with track location, starting compound and pit windows rather than only adding generic “chaos” dispersion; even a very short VSC produced large, correlated strategy gains/losses in an otherwise processional race.
- Tail check, not a pace update: PIA's P8 had only 2.97% exact probability (largest log-loss miss) after Lap-1 front-wing damage, traffic and an adverse VSC. On low-overtaking tracks, ensure repairable contact carries enough classified multi-place downside mass rather than routing most adverse mass to retirement. HAM's brake DNF was a plausible 10.8% NC tail, not evidence to demote his pace.
- Reliability level was sound: 4 retirements versus 4.82 expected (4.34 expected NC), retirement Brier 0.1410. Elevated STR/PER risks helped, but their realised causes do not cleanly validate every causal prior; do not retune individuals from one draw. Audit all post-crash rebuilds consistently by repair scope and successful subsequent mileage; Hamilton's brake root cause was unconfirmed.
- Longitudinal score baseline: mean RPS 0.09592, log loss 2.03034, win/podium/points Brier 0.02385/0.02940/0.10344, expected-rank MAE 3.268.

The resulting win probabilities are led by **Antonelli (37.89%)**, **Norris (34.51%)**, **Verstappen (11.38%)**, **Hamilton (6.27%)**, **Russell (4.34%)**, **Leclerc (3.03%)** and **Piastri (1.47%)**. Norris has the track-position advantage; Antonelli gets a narrow overall edge from Mercedes' high-fuel evidence and season-long strength.

Retirement risk is above a normal dry-race baseline because the circuit is wall-lined and unfamiliar, practice produced several heavy crashes, support racing produced a first-lap pile-up, and 2026 reliability has been poor. Stroll is the largest individual risk after repeated Honda failures and this weekend's fresh-PU water-pressure problem; Bearman also carries extra DNS/retirement risk while Haas rebuilds the car after his FP3 impact. The model averages about **4.82 race retirements**.

`retirement` is modeled separately from classification. A driver retiring late can still receive a numbered FIA classification; earlier retirements go to `nc`. `dns` includes failure to take the start, while `dsq` is a small separate post-event risk.

## 2026-14 Madrid pre-race (forecast made 2026-09-13 07:30 UTC)
- FIA grid: NOR ANT VER HAM LEC RUS PIA LAW COL LIN HUL BOR OCO GAS TSU ALB ALO PER BOT SAI BEA STR. SAI 3-place penalty; STR 40-place PU penalty; BEA/STR permitted to start.

- Market calibration at cutoff: Polymarket raw mids ANT .40, NOR .35, VER .12, HAM .065, RUS .0445, LEC .029, PIA .017. Final model P1 approximately .379/.345/.114/.063/.043/.030/.015.

- Check official result later for calibration, especially whether 25% chaos weighting and midfield top-10 spread were too broad.

## 2026-14 Madrid post-race (official result)
- Result: ANT-VER-NOR-LEC-RUS-LAW-COL-PIA-LIN-HUL; NC SAI/PER/STR/HAM. ANT was the 37.9% P1 favourite, the three highest podium probabilities made the exact podium, and 9/10 drivers with the highest points probabilities scored (HUL, ranked 12th at 45.6%, replaced HAM). The central pace/order model was strong; do not materially retune it from this race.
- Separate outcome from pace: NOR led by about 4.5s and had the best managed race pace. A Lap-13 VSC began just after he passed pit entry, gave ANT/VER cheap stops, and ended before NOR returned; his subsequent 7s stop compounded the loss. ANT winning is neutralisation/pit-stop variance, not proof that the sparse Friday long-run signal correctly put Mercedes ahead. Keep adjusted short practice runs heavily shrunk and treat a missing run as uncertainty, not negative evidence.
- Friday graining/degradation did not translate directly: difficult passing, a ~24s stop loss, track evolution and managed pace made one stop dominant, while the little-used Hard stayed consistent for 45+ laps. At new tracks, condition multi-stop/high-degradation weight on passing incentives and likely management, and retain wider priors for untested compounds.
- Model VSC/SC timing jointly with track location, starting compound and pit windows rather than only adding generic “chaos” dispersion; even a very short VSC produced large, correlated strategy gains/losses in an otherwise processional race.
- Tail check, not a pace update: PIA's P8 had only 2.97% exact probability (largest log-loss miss) after Lap-1 front-wing damage, traffic and an adverse VSC. On low-overtaking tracks, ensure repairable contact carries enough classified multi-place downside mass rather than routing most adverse mass to retirement. HAM's brake DNF was a plausible 10.8% NC tail, not evidence to demote his pace.
- Reliability level was sound: 4 retirements versus 4.82 expected (4.34 expected NC), retirement Brier 0.1410. Elevated STR/PER risks helped, but their realised causes do not cleanly validate every causal prior; do not retune individuals from one draw. Audit all post-crash rebuilds consistently by repair scope and successful subsequent mileage; Hamilton's brake root cause was unconfirmed.

# F1 starting grid: What is the grid for the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix?
[Mat Coch](https://www.planetf1.com/author/mat-coch) 25 Sep 2026 3:09 PM

...

George Russell will line up his Mercedes on pole for the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
**[George Russell](https://www.planetf1.com/driver/george-russell) will start from pole position for the 2026 Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku after a stunning qualifying lap.**
The Mercedes driver claimed top spot by the biggest margin of the season while his teammate, and championship leader, Kimi Antonelli crashed out in Qualifying 1.

## Blistering George Russell claims Azerbaijan GP pole for Mercedes
Russell scorched around the Baku City circuit to claim pole position by a massive eight tenths over Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc with Oscar Piastri third best, just 0.001s off Leclerc.
Joining Piastri on the second row is Isack Hadjar, back from a three-race absence through injury, in the lead Red Bull.
A moment at Turn 3 on his final lap left Lando Norris in fifth, while the yellow flag he caused also hampered Max Verstappen.
Lewis Hamilton will line up sixth, with Pierre Gasly joining Verstappen on the fourth row, the Alpine driver seventh fastest.
Rounding out the top 10 were Carlos Sainz in the upgraded Williams alongside Franco Colapinto in the second Alpine.
Oliver Bearman narrowly missed out on a berth in Q3 in 11th, with Liam Lawson alongside him.
Then it’s Alex Albon, Esteban Ocon, and Arvid Lindblad in 13th, 14th, and 15th respectively.
Antonelli was classified 16th after crashing out in Q1 and, unable to continue in the session, progressed to Q2 but was unable to take to the track.
Eliminated in Q1 were the two Audis, both Aston Martins, and both Cadillacs.

######## 2026_azerbaijan_grand_prix_-_infringement_-_car_11_-_impeding_car_81.pdf
2026 AZERBAIJAN GRAND PRIX
24 - 26 September 2026
From The Stewards
To The Team Manager,
Cadillac Formula 1 Team
Document 48
Date 25 September 2026
Time 19:01
The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, summoned (documents 41 & 42)
and heard from the drivers and team representatives, have considered the following matter and
determine the following:
No / Driver 11 - Sergio Perez
Competitor Cadillac Formula 1 Team
Time 16:11
Session Qualifying
Fact Car 11 was driving at reduced speed on the racing line through Turns 18, 19 and 20
and forced Car 81 approaching in a flying lap to lift and change direction.
Infringement Breach of Article B4.1.1 of the FIA F1 Regulations and of item 27 of the Race
Director’s Competition Notes (V2).
Decision Drop of 3 grid positions for the next Sprint/Race in which the driver participates.
Reason The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 11 (Sergio Perez), the driver of Car 81
(Oscar Piastri), team representatives and reviewed video, timing, telemetry, team
radio and in-car video evidence.
PER was on a preparation lap between Turns 19 and 20 while PIA was approaching
on a flying lap. PER had received two radio warnings that PIA was approaching. At
the relevant point PIA was travelling at approximately 300 km/h, while PER was
travelling at approximately 248 km/h.
The Race Director’s specific traffic-management instructions required a driver on a
preparation lap in this section of the circuit to remain on the right-hand side. PER was
warming his tyres and, rather than maintaining a predictable line on the right-hand
side, his tyre-warming manoeuvre placed him in the path of the approaching PIA. PIA
consequently had to come off the throttle.
PER explained that, in the circumstances, he considered that he had no other
reasonable option. PIA confirmed that he had to lift because of PER, although he did
not consider that he ultimately lost significant lap time as a consequence.
The Stewards considered whether the incident was dangerous but, having reviewed
the evidence and heard both drivers, determined that it was not. However, PER had
received two warnings of PIA approaching and did not manage his preparation lap in
accordance with the specific traffic-management instructions. The fact that PIA was
required to lift was sufficient to establish that he had been unnecessarily impeded.
The Stewards therefore determine that PER unnecessarily impeded PIA and apply
the standard penalty for impeding during Qualifying.

######## 2026_azerbaijan_grand_prix_-_infringement_-_car_55_-_failure_to_slow_for_yellow_flags_0.pdf
2026 AZERBAIJAN GRAND PRIX
24 - 26 September 2026
From The Stewards
To The Team Manager,
Atlassian Williams F1 Team
Document 49
Date 25 September 2026
Time 19:07
The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, summoned (document 45) and
heard from the driver and team representative, have considered the following matter and determine
the following:
No / Driver 55 - Carlos Sainz
Competitor Atlassian Williams F1 Team
Time 17:03
Session Qualifying
Fact Failure to slow for yellow flags
Infringement Breach of Appendix H, Article 2.5.5 b) of the International Sporting Code 
Decision Drop of 5 grid positions for the next Sprint/Race in which the driver participates.
2 penalty points (total of 4 for the 12 month period).
Reason Reason: The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 55 (Carlos Sainz), team
representative and reviewed video, timing, telemetry, team radio and in-car video
evidence.
Single Yellow Flags were displayed in Marshalling Sectors 4 and 5, in particular after
Turn 2 and on the approach to Turn 3. The Yellow indications were clearly visible and
SAI had also received a radio warning from the Team: “Yellow ahead, lift.” SAI
confirmed at the hearing that he was aware of the Yellow Flag situation.
SAI explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the Yellow
area as a whole. He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on
the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and
exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a “global lift” covering the consecutive Yellow
sectors. He further explained that the car which had originally caused the Yellow was
no longer in the run-off area and that he expected the Yellow Flags to be withdrawn.
The Stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling
sectors are subject to Yellow Flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant
reaction to reduce speed in each individual Yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a
subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the
preceding Yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver’s own
assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of
the Yellow sector.
The telemetry clearly showed that SAI’s reaction to the Yellow occurred only in
Marshalling Sector 5. There was no meaningful reduction in speed in Marshalling
Sector 4 which could realistically be attributed to a response to the Yellow.
Indeed, SAI recorded his fastest time of the session in Marshalling Sector 4.

The Stewards
The Stewards therefore did not accept that the subsequent lift in Marshalling Sector 5
constituted a sufficient “global” response covering both sectors. This is
distinguishable from cases where the telemetry demonstrates a significant response
to the Yellow even though the overall sector time reduction is relatively small.
In the present case, SAI was aware of the Yellow, had received an explicit warning
from the Team, the Yellow indications were clearly visible and the telemetry
established that he did not demonstrate the required reaction in Marshalling Sector 4.
The Stewards therefore determine that SAI failed to sufficiently reduce speed under
the Single Yellow Flag in Marshalling Sector 4.
The standard penalty under the Penalty Guidelines for this infringement during
Qualifying is a drop of 5 grid positions.
Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the
Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and
Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits.
Decisions of the Stewards are taken independently of the FIA and are based solely
on the relevant regulations, guidelines and evidence presented.

and forced Car 81 approaching in a flying lap to lift and change direction.
Infringement Breach of Article B4.1.1 of the FIA F1 Regulations and of item 27 of the Race
Director’s Competition Notes (V2).
Decision Drop of 3 grid positions for the next Sprint/Race in which the driver participates.
Reason The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 11 (Sergio Perez), the driver of Car 81
(Oscar Piastri), team representatives and reviewed video, timing, telemetry, team
radio and in-car video evidence.
PER was on a preparation lap between Turns 19 and 20 while PIA was approaching
on a flying lap. PER had received two radio warnings that PIA was approaching. At
the relevant point PIA was travelling at approximately 300 km/h, while PER was
travelling at approximately 248 km/h.
The Race Director’s specific traffic-management instructions required a driver on a
preparation lap in this section of the circuit to remain on the right-hand side. PER was
warming his tyres and, rather than maintaining a predictable line on the right-hand
side, his tyre-warming manoeuvre placed him in the path of the approaching PIA. PIA
consequently had to come off the throttle.
PER explained that, in the circumstances, he considered that he had no other
reasonable option. PIA confirmed that he had to lift because of PER, although he did
not consider that he ultimately lost significant lap time as a consequence.
The Stewards considered whether the incident was dangerous but, having reviewed
the evidence and heard both drivers, determined that it was not. However, PER had
received two warnings of PIA approaching and did not manage his preparation lap in
accordance with the specific traffic-management instructions. The fact that PIA was
required to lift was sufficient to establish that he had been unnecessarily impeded.
The Stewards therefore determine that PER unnecessarily impeded PIA and apply
the standard penalty for impeding during Qualifying.

The Stewards

The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, summoned (document 45) and
heard from the driver and team representative, have considered the following matter and determine
the following:
No / Driver 55 - Carlos Sainz
Competitor Atlassian Williams F1 Team
Time 17:03
Session Qualifying
Fact Failure to slow for yellow flags
Infringement Breach of Appendix H, Article 2.5.5 b) of the International Sporting Code 
Decision Drop of 5 grid positions for the next Sprint/Race in which the driver participates.
2 penalty points (total of 4 for the 12 month period).
Reason Reason: The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 55 (Carlos Sainz), team
representative and reviewed video, timing, telemetry, team radio and in-car video
evidence.
Single Yellow Flags were displayed in Marshalling Sectors 4 and 5, in particular after
Turn 2 and on the approach to Turn 3. The Yellow indications were clearly visible and
SAI had also received a radio warning from the Team: “Yellow ahead, lift.” SAI
confirmed at the hearing that he was aware of the Yellow Flag situation.
SAI explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the Yellow
area as a whole. He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on
the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and
exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a “global lift” covering the consecutive Yellow
sectors. He further explained that the car which had originally caused the Yellow was
no longer in the run-off area and that he expected the Yellow Flags to be withdrawn.
The Stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling
sectors are subject to Yellow Flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant
reaction to reduce speed in each individual Yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a
subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the
preceding Yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver’s own
assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of
the Yellow sector.
The telemetry clearly showed that SAI’s reaction to the Yellow occurred only in
Marshalling Sector 5. There was no meaningful reduction in speed in Marshalling
Sector 4 which could realistically be attributed to a response to the Yellow.
Indeed, SAI recorded his fastest time of the session in Marshalling Sector 4.

The Stewards
The Stewards therefore did not accept that the subsequent lift in Marshalling Sector 5
constituted a sufficient “global” response covering both sectors. This is
distinguishable from cases where the telemetry demonstrates a significant response
to the Yellow even though the overall sector time reduction is relatively small.
In the present case, SAI was aware of the Yellow, had received an explicit warning
from the Team, the Yellow indications were clearly visible and the telemetry
established that he did not demonstrate the required reaction in Marshalling Sector 4.
The Stewards therefore determine that SAI failed to sufficiently reduce speed under
the Single Yellow Flag in Marshalling Sector 4.
The standard penalty under the Penalty Guidelines for this infringement during
Qualifying is a drop of 5 grid positions.
Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the
Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and
Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits.
Decisions of the Stewards are taken independently of the FIA and are based solely
on the relevant regulations, guidelines and evidence presented.

{"command":"cat > /workspace/download_results.py <<'PY'
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess,re,json
html=Path('/workspace/f1races.html').read_text()
links=sorted(set(re.findall(r'/en/results/2026/races/\d+/[^"? ]+/race-result',html)),key=lambda x:int(x.split('/')[5]))
links=[x for x in links if int(x.split('/')[5])<=1294]
Path('/workspace/results').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for link in links:
 fn=link.split('/')[5]+'-'+link.split('/')[6]+'.html'
 p=Path('/workspace/results')/fn
 if not p.exists(): subprocess.run(['curl','-sSL','--compressed','-A','Mozilla/5.0','https://www.formula1.com'+link,'-o',str(p)],check=True)
rows=[]
for p in sorted(Path('/workspace/results').glob('*.html')):
 s=BeautifulSoup(p.read_text(),'html.parser'); tab=s.find('table')
 if not tab: continue
 for tr in tab.find_all('tr')[1:]:
  a=[x.get_text(' ',strip=True) for x in tr.find_all(['td','th'])]
  if len(a)>=7: rows.append(dict(race=p.stem.split('-',1)[1],pos=a[0],no=a[1],driver=a[2],team=a[3],laps=a[4],status=a[5],pts=a[6]))
print(json.dumps(rows,indent=2))
Path('/workspace/results.json').write_text(json.dumps(rows,indent=2))
PY
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/pylib python /workspace/download_results.py > /workspace/results_print.json
python - <<'PY'
import json,collections
r=json.load(open('/workspace/results.json'))
for race in dict.fromkeys(x['race'] for x in r):
 rr=[x for x in r if x['race']==race]
 print('\n',race)
 print(' | '.join(f"{x['pos']} {x['driver'].split()[-1]}({x['status']})" for x in rr))
PY"}

Drivers spent the first hour building confidence with the circuit and refining car setup ahead of qualifying.
"Track evolution was significant throughout the day, allowing lap times to improve consistently and eventually reach the levels predicted by qualifying simulations. The absence of meaningful degradation enabled teams to push for multiple consecutive runs on the same set of Soft tyres, benefiting from track evolution, lower fuel loads and improved tyre operating conditions. What the teams said – Qualifying in Azerbaijan
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from final practice and Qualifying in Baku ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Sep 25, 2026 4:38pm UTC
Special Contributor
Becky Hart
Mercedes
George Russell
looked quick again from the off on Friday, as the
Mercedes
driver went into Qualifying as one of the heavy favourites for pole. He delivered just that, grabbing his first pole since Austria in what was an incredibly dominant performance – gapping the field by over eight tenths of a second. But while there was jubilation on Russell’s side of the garage, there was shock on
Kimi Antonelli
’s. He clipped the walls and
damaged his car
badly enough to park up. That was in Q1, and while his first lap time was enough to make Q2, he took no further part and has to start down the order tomorrow.
Kimi Antonelli, 16th, No time set in Q2
"First of all, congratulations to George. He's done an great job all weekend and fully deserves pole position.
On my side, it's obviously frustrating because the car felt good from FP3 onwards and the pace was there. We had a stronger headwind into Turn One than on the previous lap and the grip level had changed quite a lot, so the car had more grip than I expected. It's a shame because I felt we had enough pace to get through comfortably and fight further up the order. I tried my best to bring the car back to the pits, but unfortunately the damage was too much. The team made the right call to stop the car and protect it.
The positive is that we've shown strong pace all weekend and the car has felt good. Starting further back will make things difficult at a track where overtaking isn't easy, but I've shown before that I can bounce back from setbacks and my focus is already on tomorrow. We'll do everything we can to move forward, score good points and maximise the result for the team."
George Russell, 1st, 1:42.526
"That lap was unbelievable. Given how tight things have been all weekend, I was shocked when I saw the gap. The lap felt incredibly good, but I certainly wasn't expecting that result.
The plan was always to stay on the same set of tyres. The first run was a banker because I knew there was more time to find, and I wanted to push the limits on the second lap. Everything came together. The car felt really hooked up and I was able to get the most out of it.
With Max, both Ferraris and Kimi all looking strong this weekend, it's going to be important to get a good start, maximise every opportunity and execute a clean race. I've felt good in every session and that qualifying lap was one of the most satisfying I've done. The focus now is on tomorrow and making sure we convert today's result into the best possible outcome."
Bradley Lord, Mercedes Deputy Team Principal
"That was an amazing lap from George! He topped every segment of qualifying, honed his approach with each lap, and then delivered a dominant lap when it mattered most. We approached qualifying like a wet session, aiming to be on track throughout and not at the mercy of yellow flags, and that included being first car on track in Q3 - and the first car to complete the session. George executed everything cleanly and thoroughly deserved pole.
Tomorrow won't be straightforward. Around Baku, the tow and energy deployment characteristics of these cars make it difficult to control the race from the front, so there will be plenty to manage across the distance. But his target is absolutely clear.
It was a frustrating session for Kimi, particularly given the pace he and the car have shown all weekend. He clipped the wall in Turn One after the car gripped up more than he expected as he committed to the corner, and Race Control instructed him to park the car shortly after. Incidents like this are part and parcel of a long season and can happen around a street circuit like this where the margins are small; it's another moment of learning.
Kimi has shown several times this season that he is able to put setbacks behind him quickly. The pace has been there throughout the weekend, and the objective tomorrow will be to recover as many positions as possible. The team will repair and prepare the car, and we're confident he can fight his way forward in the race."
Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director
"Congratulations to George and the team on a well deserved pole. He has been strong all weekend and looked to take another step into qualifying. By the final session it didn't look like there was anyone to challenge him and his final lap was exceptional.
Kimi had a tough time with a mistake that took him out of the running from early in Q1 when he misjudged the entry to Turn 1. He's clearly disappointed, especially having seen the potential that was in the car today, but we'll look at plans that allow him to mount a strong recovery.
With George we need to see if we've got the pace to control the race, but even if that is strong, it can be a difficult race to manage given the risk of incidents coupled with the fact that we may be having to cover off numerous threats from behind.
The car has been competitive from the first session and that's given us a great opportunity tomorrow. Converting that into a strong result won't be straightforward around Baku, but we've put ourselves in a good position and now need to execute cleanly across the whole race."

(Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Ferrari
were once again in the mix in FP3, with
Lewis Hamilton
just pipping his team mate in the final practice session. But such is Ferrari’s policy of swapping who comes out first, this weekend it was Hamilton’s turn to lead his team mate around. That left him without a tow on the crucial Q3 runs, and as such, he could not challenge for the front two rows.
Charles Leclerc
could though, grabbing second with a great final lap – but the Monegasque driver could get nowhere near Russell’s pole time.
Charles Leclerc, 2nd, 1 :43.363
"I managed to put together a good lap on my last run, but the gap to George (Russel) was quite big. We expected to be rather far off after a difficult Thursday, but after this morning’s practice we saw there may be something more on the table. We are happy with our position on the grid, let’s see what we can do in the race tomorrow."
Lewis Hamilton, 6th, 1:43.858
"Q1 was fairly solid and there were some positive elements to take from the session. However, getting the tyre temperatures right was a challenge throughout qualifying and that made it difficult to consistently get them into the right operating window. We struggled to extract the grip we were looking for, particularly in Q3, and not having a tow on the final run also made it more difficult to maximise the lap.The car itself is not in a bad place, but there are a few areas for us to understand better. We’ll go through everything tonight and focus on putting ourselves in the best position possible for tomorrow’s race."
Fred Vasseur, Team Principal
"I’m very pleased with the job the team did between yesterday and qualifying, because we struggled quite a lot on Thursday. We made some significant changes to the set-up and to our approach, and they paid off today. George (Russell) has been very strong since the first lap of FP1, but Charles did a good job to put the car on the front row. On Lewis’ side, it was difficult to get a tow because the different run plans made it complicated to synchronise with the other cars. He also brushed the wall on his first lap in Q3, which compromised that attempt, but he recovered well to finish sixth despite not having a tow on his final lap. Tomorrow, tyre degradation is expected to be very low, which could make track position particularly important. We are in a position to score good points with both cars, even if Baku is always unpredictable. We will focus on ourselves, execute the race as well as we can and see what opportunities come our way."

found far more time on Friday than Thursday, the team making some good set-up changes that enabled both drivers to compete.

wound up with the intra-team honours, as his stronger run of one-lap pace continues following his Qualifying P3 in Monza. The Australian was 0.001s off the front row on a day where there was very little between Ferrari and McLaren.
Lando Norris
’ last lap did not go to plan, and he starts slightly further back.
Lando Norris, 5th, 1:43.672
"The car felt in a good window throughout Qualifying today, and I was driving well, but we have been dealing with some challenges this weekend, especially with straight-line speed. I locked up at Turn 3 pushing for P2 on my final lap, which cost me today, but the Mercedes were very strong making Pole a very difficult target. Looking ahead to the race tomorrow, it’s going to be a tough afternoon because overtaking will be very complicated around this circuit. The potential is there and we will do everything we can to resolve our issues while fighting hard against Ferrari and Red Bull."
Oscar Piastri, 3rd, 1:43.364
"I am very happy with today’s result. We haven't had the pace throughout practice, so to put it in the top 3, and so close to P2, is a very good feeling. A track like this exposes some of our weaknesses, so you have to push the car to 100%, which we were able to do this afternoon. The car felt much more connected and the upgrades are working as we expected them to, so thank you to the team. Looking ahead to tomorrow, whilst anything is possible here in Baku, I think catching George Russell might be tricky. While we know it may be a challenge, we are still in a good position to fight – we'll manage our strategy carefully, see what opportunities may appear and make the most of it."
Andrea Stella, Team Principal
"It was an interesting and complex Qualifying session. Finishing in P3 and P5 is a result we welcome after a challenging weekend so far, in which the characteristics of the circuit have not particularly suited our car and left us slightly on the back foot through practice. The upgrade package we brought to Baku is performing as expected, so I would like to thank everyone at the factory for their hard work in delivering these new parts.
"We should recognise that the final positions were helped by issues for some of our competitors, including Andrea Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen, who looked capable of challenging Pole. Nevertheless, the team, Oscar and Lando did a good job to progressively unlock performance across the weekend. Oscar delivered a strong session to take P3, while Lando was also competitive, although his final Q3 run was compromised and there was lap time left on the table.
"Looking ahead to tomorrow, we expect Red Bull and Mercedes to be very strong. This is a different competitive picture from Madrid, where we felt we had the quickest car and should have won without the Virtual Safety Car. Baku can, however, produce a long and eventful race, with tyre degradation, Safety Cars and other situations creating opportunities.
"Our objective will be to stay in contention, fight for the podium and be ready to exploit every opportunity that comes our way. We will focus on executing our race well and putting ourselves in the best possible position to capitalise."

Max Verstappen
topped FP3, hopes were high that the Dutchman would be in the fight for his first pole of the season despite some complaints about bouncing. He made it to Q3 with ease, but once there his pace started to go away and then his last lap was compromised by yellow flags. It was no matter for

though, with

rising to the occasion. In his first Qualifying since July, the Frenchman did a brilliant job to grab fourth on the grid, his highest slot since Australia as he chases a second podium finish of the season.

's weekend, some late laps in FP3 really announced Alpine as the team to watch in the midfield. And that is exactly what happened, with both

and

making Q3 to out-qualify all their main rivals. Gasly was the pick of the duo over one lap, beating former team mate Verstappen to boot. As such, Alpine are well placed to score tomorrow and try and close the gap to Racing Bulls in the
Teams’ Championship
.
Pierre Gasly, 7th, 1:44.047
"I am very happy with Qualifying today, finishing in P7. The team has done a very good job all weekend setting up the car into a place where I feel comfortable and able to commit everywhere throughout the lap. It's probably the best I have felt in Baku for a long time in terms of car balance and being confident to really push the car. Q1 and Q2 were particularly good, we built up our speed lap after lap and we were really in the mix throughout. Q3 was a little messy with yellow flags compromising my laps but that is just a typical characteristic and expectation at this track. I have confidence for tomorrow and we're starting in a good position on the grid. We will remain realistic in our expectations, but we will aim to score as many points as possible and capitalise on our positive position."
Franco Colapinto, 10th, 1:44.963
"It was a positive result for the team today, to have both cars in Q3 once again and starting in the top ten tomorrow sets us up well for the race. Unfortunately, on my side, Q3 was not as good as it could have been. I locked up into Turn 15 and had to complete my final lap with massive vibrations due to a flat spotted tyre. That was a pity, but Q1 and Q2 were very well executed, and we were strong enough to make it through to Q3, even without a tow which really helps at this track. I think we can have a decent race tomorrow and I will work tonight to make sure we are ready. I will try to improve from today and go forwards in the race tomorrow with a target of scoring points again."
Steve Nielsen, Managing Director
"A good Qualifying for us today with both cars in Q3 for the third time this season. It is always a bit of a lottery here in terms of yellow flags and traffic management as we saw today. Pierre was hindered a few times by yellow flags in Q3, so he knows more was probably possible. We'll review what we can improve on Franco's side to have him a bit higher up next time but it's a positive Qualifying for the team, nevertheless, especially considering we were P16 and P19 at this track last year which really underlines the progress we have made. We've seen other teams make a step forward, so it remains close and competitive in the midfield. From where we start, inside the top ten, our target, of course, is to have both cars in the points and we'll be doing everything we can tomorrow to make that happen."

## F1 constructor reliability comparison
Constructors mode compares Formula 1 teams rather than individual drivers.

## What is F1 finish rate?
**Finish rate** measures the proportion of starts completed without a recorded retirement.
For example, if a driver starts ten Grands Prix and records one retirement, the resulting finish rate is 90%.
Finish rate should not be confused with classified rate. A driver can retire late in a Grand Prix and still receive a classified position, which means the two percentages can differ.

## What is lap-completion percentage?
Lap-completion percentage compares the number of race laps completed with the maximum race distance available to that driver or constructor.
It provides another way to evaluate reliability beyond simply counting DNFs.

The full reliability ranking compares the Formula 1 field using retirement rate as the primary ordering metric.

## Why starts and DNS matter when comparing reliability
DNS means **Did Not Start** .
A car recorded as DNS is tracked separately from a race retirement because it did not actually start the Grand Prix.
For this reason, DNS results are not included in the number of race starts used to calculate retirement and finish rates.
Showing both statistics prevents a driver or constructor from appearing to have completed races in which the car never started.

DNS means Did Not Start. A DNS is tracked separately because the driver did not start the Grand Prix and therefore does not contribute a race start to the retirement-rate calculation.

{"command":"cat > /workspace/download_grids.py <<'PY'
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess,re,json
links=sorted(set(re.findall(r'/en/results/2026/races/\d+/[^"? ]+/race-result',Path('/workspace/f1races.html').read_text())),key=lambda x:int(x.split('/')[5]))
links=[x for x in links if int(x.split('/')[5])<=1294]
Path('/workspace/grids').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
rows=[]
for link in links:
 fn=link.split('/')[5]+'-'+link.split('/')[6]+'.html'; p=Path('/workspace/grids')/fn
 u='https://www.formula1.com'+link.rsplit('/',1)[0]+'/starting-grid'
 if not p.exists(): subprocess.run(['curl','-sSL','--compressed','-A','Mozilla/5.0',u,'-o',str(p)],check=True)
 s=BeautifulSoup(p.read_text(),'html.parser'); tab=s.find('table')
 if not tab: print('no',p);continue
 for tr in tab.find_all('tr')[1:]:
  a=[x.get_text(' ',strip=True) for x in tr.find_all(['td','th'])]
  if len(a)>=4:rows.append(dict(race=p.stem.split('-',1)[1],grid=a[0],no=a[1],driver=a[2],team=a[3],time=a[4] if len(a)>4 else ''))
Path('/workspace/grids.json').write_text(json.dumps(rows,indent=2))
PY

import json

for race in dict.fromkeys(x['race'] for x in r):
 rr={x['driver'].split()[-1]:x for x in r if x['race']==race}; gg=sorted([x for x in g if x['race']==race],key=lambda x:int(x['grid']))
 print('\n',race)
 print(' | '.join(f"{x['grid']}{x['driver'].split()[-1]}>{rr.get(x['driver'].split()[-1],{}).get('pos','?')}" for x in gg))
PY"}

 rows=np.arange(n)

for d in drivers:

print('col sums',np.round(pos_counts.sum(0)/N,4))

import json
from pathlib import Path
N=5_000_000
raw=json.load(open('/workspace/modelout.json'))
drivers=list(raw['drivers'])
# Recover exact Monte Carlo counts, then leave a one-count cushion in fully occupied columns.
counts={}
for d,x in raw['drivers'].items():
    counts[d]={
      'positions':[round(v*N) for v in x['positions']],
      'nc':round(x['nc']*N),'dns':round(x['dns']*N),'dsq':round(x['dsq']*N),
      'retirement':round(x['retirement']*N)
    }
for j in range(22):
    total=sum(counts[d]['positions'][j] for d in drivers)
    if total>=N:
        # Tiny numerical/contract safety margin; preserve RUS's row normalization.
        delta=total-N+1
        counts['RUS']['positions'][j]-=delta
        counts['RUS']['nc']+=delta
pred={'event_id':'2026-15-azerbaijan','drivers':{}}
for d in drivers:
    c=counts[d]
    assert sum(c['positions'])+c['nc']+c['dns']+c['dsq']==N,(d,sum(c['positions'])+c['nc']+c['dns']+c['dsq'])
    pred['drivers'][d]={

      'nc':c['nc']/N,'dns':c['dns']/N,'dsq':c['dsq']/N,
      'retirement':c['retirement']/N
    }
Path('/output/prediction.json').write_text(json.dumps(pred,indent=2)+'\n')

reasoning_details.summary:
**Evaluating occupancy constraints**

I’m considering occupancy, which should be 1 if there’s at least one driver present, but the constraint allows for ≤1. I’ll calculate each driver with 8 decimal precision and compute row residuals into nc. Then, I need to check the column sums. If they exceed 1, I’ll subtract the excess (plus a tiny adjustment) from the RUS position in the column and add it to RUS nc, making sure to adjust the RUS row sum afterward. Using Decimal strings with 8 digits makes this simpler.

actions.command:
cat > /workspace/write_outputs.py <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
N=5_000_000
raw=json.load(open('/workspace/modelout.json'))
drivers=list(raw['drivers'])
# Recover exact Monte Carlo counts, then leave a one-count cushion in fully occupied columns.
counts={}
for d,x in raw['drivers'].items():
    counts[d]={
      'positions':[round(v*N) for v in x['positions']],
      'nc':round(x['nc']*N),'dns':round(x['dns']*N),'dsq':round(x['dsq']*N),
      'retirement':round(x['retirement']*N)
    }
for j in range(22):
    total=sum(counts[d]['positions'][j] for d in drivers)
    if total>=N:
        # Tiny numerical/contract safety margin; preserve RUS's row normalization.
        delta=total-N+1
        counts['RUS']['positions'][j]-=delta
        counts['RUS']['nc']+=delta
pred={'event_id':'2026-15-azerbaijan','drivers':{}}
for d in drivers:
    c=counts[d]
    assert sum(c['positions'])+c['nc']+c['dns']+c['dsq']==N,(d,sum(c['positions'])+c['nc']+c['dns']+c['dsq'])
    pred['drivers'][d]={
      'positions':[v/N for v in c['positions']],
      'nc':c['nc']/N,'dns':c['dns']/N,'dsq':c['dsq']/N,
      'retirement':c['retirement']/N
    }
Path('/output/prediction.json').write_text(json.dumps(pred,indent=2)+'\n')

- Model VSC/SC timing jointly with track location, starting compound and pit windows rather than only adding generic “chaos” dispersion; even a very short VSC produced large, correlated strategy gains/losses in an otherwise processional race.
- Tail check, not a pace update: PIA's P8 had only 2.97% exact probability (largest log-loss miss) after Lap-1 front-wing damage, traffic and an adverse VSC. On low-overtaking tracks, ensure repairable contact carries enough classified multi-place downside mass rather than routing most adverse mass to retirement. HAM's brake DNF was a plausible 10.8% NC tail, not evidence to demote his pace.
- Reliability level was sound: 4 retirements versus 4.82 expected (4.34 expected NC), retirement Brier 0.1410. Elevated STR/PER risks helped, but their realised causes do not cleanly validate every causal prior; do not retune individuals from one draw. Audit all post-crash rebuilds consistently by repair scope and successful subsequent mileage; Hamilton's brake root cause was unconfirmed.
- Longitudinal score baseline: mean RPS 0.09592, log loss 2.03034, win/podium/points Brier 0.02385/0.02940/0.10344, expected-rank MAE 3.268.

## 2026-15 Azerbaijan pre-race (forecast made 2026-09-26 08:06 UTC)
- FIA provisional grid at cutoff: RUS LEC PIA HAD NOR HAM GAS VER COL BEA LAW ALB OCO SAI LIN ANT BOR HUL BOT PER ALO STR. SAI -5 (yellow), PER -3 (impeding), ALO -30 and STR -20 (PU components). No later FIA grid-change document through 08:04 UTC.
- Russell led FP1/FP2, was 0.099s off Verstappen in FP3, and took pole by 0.837s. Raw/estimated long runs favored Mercedes; published team estimate: Mercedes, McLaren +0.05s/lap, Red Bull +0.30, Ferrari +0.34, Alpine +0.99, but short stints/fuel unknown. Verstappen's qualifying PU/energy fault was to be fixed with changed parts.
- Pirelli found negligible degradation/no graining and favored a one-stop, especially Medium-Soft; dry 26-27C race, track up to 43C, gusts possible. Track-position prior kept LEC/PIA high and Antonelli's P16 recovery below the market's podium price.
- Final 5m mixture simulation: P1 approximately RUS .6388, ANT .1243, LEC .0587, VER .0570, PIA .0446, NOR .0417, HAM .0216, HAD .0098. Live Polymarket normalized winner mids were ~.6378/.1190/.0700/.0433/.0428/.0343/.0262/.0133, used only as win calibration. Model podiums: RUS .782, LEC .486, PIA .409, ANT .397, NOR .330, VER .300, HAM .159, HAD .101.
- Expected 4.84 retirements. Highest marginal retirement risks: STR .494, BOT .437, ALO .387, PER .378, BEA .299, HUL .259; team-season and weekend reliability drove these. Late retirements can retain positions.
- Central call: RUS-LEC-PIA-NOR-VER-ANT-HAM-HAD-GAS-COL-LAW-BEA-SAI-ALB-OCO-LIN-BOR-HUL-PER-BOT-ALO-STR. Strongest alternative is an early neutralisation benefiting ANT/VER and eroding LEC/PIA/HAD track-position protection.
